programs: STS BA and BS (one set of outcomes on file)

outcomes.text: Students will analyze a topic in ways that makes connections across diverse disciplines.
outcomes.codes: Cognitive verb only (analyze). Recorded, never counted.
outcomes.site: STS 214 and the STS 403 capstone (named in the unit's proposal)

outcomes.text: Students will explain and apply key STS concepts, theories, practices, and methodological approaches.
outcomes.codes: Cognitive verb only (explain). Recorded, never counted.

example.outcome: Students will analyze a topic in ways that makes connections across diverse disciplines.
example.site: STS 214 (proposed unit on AI's material and systemic dimensions) and the STS 403 capstone project and presentation
example.who: STS 403 instructor and the capstone committee
example.act: Write an analysis tracing a technology across historical, ethical, and material accounts, and present it to peers
example.model: A model produces a fluent cross-disciplinary synthesis on request. As filed, the outcome gives a reader no way to distinguish a student's analysis from a generated one, while a generated synthesis omits what the student chose to connect and why. EAB's findings on AI competencies in the occupations STS graduates enter belong here.
example.reason: The analysis is the judgment the degree certifies. Students are permitted to use a model to locate sources and to test their own synthesis against a generated one. They write the analysis themselves and state what the tool supplied, what it left out, and why they kept or rejected it.
example.revised: Students will write and present an analysis of a technology connecting historical, ethical, and material accounts across disciplines, and will state the reasons for their decisions about any AI use in producing it.

literacy.describe: In STS the system under description is also the object of study. A large language model predicts likely text from a corpus assembled by particular firms, trained with particular labor, and run on particular infrastructure. Describing it in the unit's own terms means naming the acts the outcomes ask of students (tracing a technology across accounts, explaining a concept, applying a method) and saying which of those acts a model performs on the surface.
literacy.analyze: The structural question is the field's home ground: whose data, labor, energy, and interests the tool carries into a student's analysis, and what a generated synthesis leaves out of an account of a sociotechnical system. The proposed STS 214 unit on AI's material and systemic dimensions places this analysis in the curriculum as content. The Accelerator asks the unit to apply the same analysis to its own assignments.
literacy.decide: The operative question is which acts are the judgment the STS degree certifies, and what the program says about a tool supplying the surface of those acts. For each outcome the Lab records the decision and the reason the program gives for it, counting refusal with a reason as a decision.

policy_intro: CWSP read the unit-level record at NC State's twelve official peers and the land-grant set used for FER, then the disciplinary societies and the nearest STS-type departments outside both sets. For each document, the entry gives its scope and CWSP's reading of where its language breaks down, offered for the working group to correct.
policy_finding: At the unit level the peer record is silent, since the two STS units among NC State's peers (Virginia Tech and UC Davis) have issued no AI policy and defer to campus guidance. Neither 4S nor SHOT has taken a position, although both now host panels on generative AI in teaching and research. The nearest unit-level texts come from outside the peer set, where departments have chosen four different genres: a set of default rules (Stony Brook), a clause folding AI into plagiarism (Georgia Tech), a declaration of principle for the humanities and social sciences (Cambridge), and a prohibition with a dissertation affirmation (Columbia History). NC State STS would write the first STS-specific statement among its peers, with the choice of genre open.

policies.unit: Department of Technology, AI and Society
policies.doc: Policy for Using Generative AI and Large Language Models
policies.peer: Outside the peer and land-grant sets
policies.says: Seven default rules for courses and department work: attribution with software, version, and prompts, no wholesale substitution, limited use in serious academic work, students able to explain their work in person, and the policy on every syllabus.
policies.glitch: Although the department says it updates the page regularly, it gives no date, so readers have no way to tell which edition governs a given term. Because the rule limits use in "serious academic work" without defining the phrase, each reader draws the line alone.

policies.unit: School of History and Sociology (MS and PhD, History and Sociology of Technology and Science)
policies.says: One clause, under the written comprehensive exam: plagiarism includes inappropriate use of AI technologies.
policies.glitch: Because the school left "inappropriate" undefined and placed the clause under one examination, its graduate students find no AI rule for coursework, the thesis, or the dissertation.

policies.unit: Department of Science, Technology, and Society
policies.says: Silent at the unit level. University guidance (TLOS, Responsible and Ethical AI Principles) applies.
policies.glitch: A department whose subject is the governance of technology governs its own students' use of one through principles written for the whole university.

policies.says: Silent at the unit level. The campus Code of Academic Conduct treats AI use without instructor permission as misconduct, and the campus does not require syllabus AI statements.
policies.glitch: Misconduct turns on instructor permission, and no document is required to state it, so a student's standing depends on a statement the course is not obliged to write.

policies.unit: School of the Humanities and Social Sciences
policies.doc: Manifesto and Principles for Generative AI in Scholarship
policies.says: Asks if, rather than how, generative AI contributes to scholarship. Includes a student declaration template and a sample rubric.
policies.glitch: The School's authors move the question from procedure to warrant, the move this workbook asks of each row, yet the declaration template they supply records use without the reasons for it.

policies.says: Students should not use generative AI to create submitted text, including theses. Dissertations carry an affirmation of no AI-created text. Research uses are discussed with advisers and cited.
policies.glitch: The department wrote its rule against a product (AI-created text) and left the line between created text and assisted research to conversations with advisers, outside the policy itself.

policies.doc: No society statement on generative AI found
policies.says: Neither society has issued a position. 4S 2026 hosts an open panel on generative AI including refusal. SHOT held a 2025 roundtable on AI in teaching the history of technology, and its 2026 meeting invites workshops on the subject.
policies.glitch: The field discusses the question at its meetings and leaves the decision to departments, which places the first disciplinary statement with a unit such as NC State STS.

program_rows.reading: Silent in the record. Two outcomes on file, both cognitive (analyze a topic across disciplines, explain and apply STS concepts), and neither names the writing or presentation in which a student shows the analysis. The program sits one sentence from documenting what it teaches. The proposal's first intended outcome, revised program outcomes naming critical AI analysis, is the sentence the record is missing.

plain_finding: No STS department among NC State's peers has an AI policy of its own, and neither of the field's two societies (4S and SHOT) has issued one. The nearest examples come from other universities and take four different forms, so NC State STS is free to choose the form its own statement takes.
